title: A Dating App Is Offering ‘Chivalry Mode’ and ‘Marriage Timeline’ to Get Gen Z Married
gist: Match Group has relaunched its Christian dating app Upward as a marriage-focused app for Gen Z, adding features like Chivalry Mode and Marriage Timeline. The pivot rests on its 2026 Singles in America finding that 72% of Gen Z want to marry. Researcher Daniel Cox disputes the premise, citing Pew data on falling interest in marriage, especially among young women. Users also report a mismatch between the app's conservative user base and its broader positioning, and Upward would not disclose active-user numbers.

themes.theme: Upward relaunch strategy at Match Group

insights.claim: Match Group relaunched Upward around two findings from its 2026 Singles in America study. The first is that 72% of Gen Z want to get married. The second is that a quarter of singles aged 18-34 identify with traditional values around family, faith and community.
insights.speaker: Jason Parham
insights.so_what: Match is repositioning niche apps around values-based segments to look for growth outside Tinder and Hinge.

insights.claim: Upward moved away from being an app exclusively for Christian daters in order to appeal to people who share marriage goals but "may not lead with a faith-first mindset," according to Match brand marketing director Lauren DeFord.
insights.speaker: Lauren DeFord
insights.so_what: Widening the addressable market risks putting off the core Christian user base.

insights.claim: Falling engagement and the arrival of AI have pushed dating companies to rethink user growth, and some are abandoning their original mission. Upward's expansion is one example.
insights.speaker: Jason Parham
insights.so_what: Dating-app engagement is in structural decline, which drives pivots across Match Group's portfolio.
insights.quote: Dwindling engagement and the introduction of AI have pushed companies to reassess user growth.

insights.claim: Upward runs on tiered subscriptions with Tinder-style swiping. New features include Chivalry Mode, which nudges men to message first as Bumble used to, and Marriage Timeline, which lets users share when they hope to marry.
insights.speaker: Jason Parham
insights.so_what: Product differentiation through intent-signaling features is a monetization lever for subscription tiers.
insights.locator: Upward, which runs on a tiered subscription

insights.claim: Upward declined to share its number of active users. Since its 2020 debut it has had functionality and perception problems, with Apple App Store reviews complaining of poor support, weak filters and automatic bans.
insights.speaker: Jason Parham
insights.so_what: Refusing to disclose user numbers suggests limited traction for a small asset within Match's portfolio.

insights.claim: Upward's relaunch marketing uses an "Americana" theme and a Western-style "Wanted: For Life" campaign, with videos captioned "chivalrymaxxing".
insights.speaker: Jason Parham
insights.so_what: The branding targets the trad cultural trend and leans into polarized identity marketing.

themes.theme: Skepticism about Gen Z marriage demand

insights.claim: Daniel Cox argues that Gen Z is not returning to traditional relationship norms. A decline in social and civic life has produced a hyperindividualistic culture that deprioritizes marriage, so fewer Gen Zs are coupling up.
insights.speaker: Daniel Cox
insights.so_what: This undercuts the demand thesis behind marriage-focused dating products.

insights.claim: An American Institute for Boys and Men survey found that 44% of Gen Z men had no relationship experience at all during their teen years, double the rate for older men.
insights.speaker: Jason Parham
entities: American Institute for Boys and Men
insights.so_what: Young men's withdrawal from dating shrinks the active user pool for dating apps.

insights.claim: Pew found in 2023 that only 23% of adults saw marriage as extremely or very important to a fulfilling life, compared with 61% for close friends. The share of high school seniors expecting to marry fell from 80% in 1993 to 67% in 2023, driven mainly by young women.
insights.speaker: Jason Parham
insights.so_what: The long-term decline in the value placed on marriage works against products built around marriage.

insights.claim: Cox expects young women's declining desire to marry to continue, because of a growing belief that marriage makes them less happy than staying single.
insights.speaker: Daniel Cox
insights.so_what: A dating app that depends on women's demand for marriage faces a lasting gender mismatch.
insights.quote: There’s increasingly a belief among young women that marriage makes them less happy
insights.locator: The trend is likely to continue

insights.claim: Cox sees the trad trend as a reaction to the lack of cultural norms around courtship. Daters want a clear script as nontraditional arrangements such as polyamory and relationship anarchy grow among young people.
insights.speaker: Daniel Cox
insights.so_what: Demand for structured, role-defined dating products may be real but niche.
insights.quote: People are wanting something over nothing
insights.locator: Cox, who is the director of the Survey Center

insights.claim: Cox says Match's finding that 72% of Gen Z want to marry may be inflated, because younger respondents are less likely to have already married or divorced than millennials or Gen Xers. Match's survey sampled 5,000 unpartnered US singles.
insights.speaker: Daniel Cox
insights.so_what: Company-sponsored surveys used to justify product pivots should be read skeptically.

insights.claim: Users report that Upward is dominated by conservative "MAGA types" while also offering hookup-app features such as body-type fields, allowing married users, and offering "I'm not into labels" relationship options. Liberal Christians and strict-Christian users are both alienated.
insights.speaker: Jason Parham
insights.so_what: Positioning the app between two audiences could push churn up on both sides.
insights.quote: I did not know me being Christian and leaning liberal was a big ask

insights.claim: Some Christian users say the pivot dilutes Upward's faith focus. Match's Lauren DeFord says Christian singles remain core and can still match by denomination and practice.
insights.speaker: Lauren DeFord
insights.so_what: Keeping the core base while expanding the audience is the main execution risk for the relaunch.
